result: Rain taps against the windowpane in a rhythm older than language itself. I watch droplets race down the glass, blurring the street below into watercolors of gray and gold. There is strange comfort in weather that asks nothing of me. It simply arrives, does what must be done, and leaves. I think of all the mornings like this that passed through cities, and quiet kitchens long before mine. People made coffee while storms brewed. They read dog-eared paperbacks. They stared at walls, wondering if they were doing enough. And yet, the rain fell on them all the same. That is the quiet miracle of ordinary moments: they refuse to glorify themselves, but they hold us equally. I press my palm flat against the cool sill. Somewhere down the block, a bicycle bell rings. A cat shakes water from its fur in a sudden, dignified spray. Nothing is particularly significant here, and yet everything is. We spend so much time chasing milestones, mistaking volume for meaning. But maybe meaning lives in the pause between heartbeats, in the steam rising from cup, in the way light catches dust motes dancing above an empty chair. The air smells like wet pavement and old paper. I let it in. Time softens at the edges. I breathe. Consider how a single hour contains multitudes. The kettle whistles. A neighbor laughs. A leaf detaches and spirals to the ground. None demands recognition, yet it all matters. The earth asks only that we notice.
